Bette wolgezieret zugericht, und globte I. F. G. dem Herrn von Rosenberg an Statt der Kays. Maytt. bey dero Fürstl. Würden an, sich aus dem Zimmer nicht zu begeben, biss auff I. K. Unkosten, und hatten auss I. K. M. Keller täglich 10. Pfund Wein, und Bier die Nothdurfft; es mochte zu I. F. G. gehen, wer da wolte. Eine Gvardie ward bald I. F. G. von 4. Trabanten, so Tag und Nacht wacheten, verordnet. Wie nu der von Rosenberg dies alles verricht, nimbt er von I. F. G. sein Ab- schiedt, tröstet I. F. G., sie solten sich gedulden, I. K. M. würden die Sachen in kurtzen auff andere Mittel richten, darzu er denn ein guter Beförderer sein wolte, und giengen wider zu I. K. Maytt uber den Gang. Uber solchem vornehmenden Aussgang wird Schweinichen dem Hoffemeister nicht wol, dieweil er seinen Herren sahe gefänglich, seinen Gesellen den Cantzler ingleichen in weissen Thurn setzen. Hanns Lossatte hatte sich auch verlohren, und wuste nicht, wo er hinkommen war, weil er bey seinem Herren wie der Haase beym Peucker hafftete. Nichts desto weniger folgete er seinem Herrn mit grossem Hertzeleid nach. Wie nu der Herr von Rosenberg von Hertzog Hennerichen die Stiegen beynn grossen Saal wider runter gehet, fraget der Herr von Rosenberg: seinen Marschall den Mettigen. Wo sein LandsMann Schweinichen der Lig- nitsche Hoffmeister sey? Welche Worte der von Schweinichen wol hörete, die ihme denn sein Hertze brachen; vermeinete nichts anders, es würde ihm auch also wie den andern gehen. Und weil er es nicht anders machen konte, tringet er durch das Gedrängnüss, und giebet sich bey dem Herrn von Rosenberg selbst an, den denn der von Rosenberg wol kante, both der Herr von Rosenberg ihm so bald die Faust, sagende: Ich habe ein treues Mittleiden mit eurem Herren, auch mit euch selbst. Ihr aber dürfft euch keiner Kays. Ungnade befahren, ihr habet einen gnädigen Kayser, ich habe derowegen nach euch gefraget, dass ich euch anmelden wolte, dass I. K. M. euren Herren gnädigst mit 8. Dienern speisen wird lassen, und wo ihr solches abholen sollet lassen, dass wird euch mein Marschall anweisen. Ihr sollet euch zu mir aller Gnade und gutter Beförderung getrösten, und wo ihr euch bey mir auffhalten wollet, so wollet solches dem Herrn Mettichen vertrauen. So sehr nu der Hoffemeister er schrocken worden, so sehr war er der Reden froh, und sagte derowegen dem Herrn von Rosenberg höchsten Danck, Hess sich also, wo sein gefangener Fürst und Herr Tranck und Essen abholen solte, anweisen. entries.english:
Chapter 51. Duke Heinrich’s reply.

In response to these grave accusations, and because of the Emperor’s extreme displeasure, His Princely Grace was deeply distressed, though he recovered somewhat and recalled that most of the matters alleged had also arisen during the war in Silesia. He told the imperial officers that he had heard with the greatest grief and sorrow of the serious charges the Roman Emperor was making against him and of the Emperor’s displeasure, which—he hoped, without sufficient cause—his enemies and ill-wishers had provoked with reports they could never prove. He admitted none of the charges as described or intended, and said they could not be demonstrated. He humbly begged the Emperor either to hear him together with his false accusers or to allow him to answer the charges and establish his innocence. He was certain that, if the Emperor graciously heard his explanation, it would satisfy him.

He trusted that so just an Emperor would not condemn him without a proper hearing and opportunity to answer. The Emperor should also remember the loyal and obedient services he had rendered: attending coronations and princely weddings, the imperial funeral, the campaign in Hungary against the Turks, and the subsequent journey to the Imperial Diet, all at great expense and out of dutiful obedience. He had never opposed the Emperor; even when deprived of lands and people on the basis of false reports, he had remained obedient. If these things were considered, the Emperor’s displeasure would abate and he would graciously refrain from the threatened execution. If, after a full hearing, he were found guilty on any point, he would submit to the Emperor’s punishment, but asked on his princely honor to remain until the Emperor had heard and ruled on every charge. He therefore begged the officers to present his apology and petition and to ask the Emperor not to execute him or condemn him unheard.

Herr von Rosenberg reported that the officers had heard the Duke’s apology and petition on the Emperor’s behalf and would present them and do what they could for him. They soon returned. Herr von Rosenberg said the Emperor ordered His Princely Grace to submit to obedience; although his objections, apology, and petition had been presented, the Emperor had already issued a considered decree and would not revoke it. The Duke was to obey the earlier order; the Emperor would nevertheless deliberate further and later inform him of his decision. When Duke Heinrich tried again to establish his innocence, the officers interrupted him: they had orders to hear no more on the merits and, on the Emperor’s behalf, urged him to stop and submit.

Duke Heinrich replied that the Emperor was so just that he would not condemn even a poor sinner unheard, much less condemn him without a full hearing. He again asked the Emperor to hear him, saying that he had not deserved what was being done to him. Just as the Emperor wished God to hear him, he should also hear the Duke and not close his just ear. As a prince and estate of Silesia, he could invoke his princely privileges and appear with the Emperor before the princely court, and before everyone else there, if necessary. If this reasonable request went unheard, he would have to lament the great injustice to God in heaven and pray for justice. The officers made no reply. Herr von Rosenberg repeated that the Emperor’s order was for His Princely Grace to submit and that they had no further authority to discuss the case. Herr von Rosenberg then took Duke Heinrich by the hand and led him away. In the middle of the room he stopped and called out that the Emperor’s express order also required Hanns Schrame, Duke Heinrich’s chancellor, to submit and follow the castle captain. When the captain did not know which man was the Chancellor of Liegnitz, Brandano von Zedlitz pointed him out. The castle captain immediately took Schrame into custody and, without a hearing, had him led to the White Tower.

Herr von Rosenberg went with the imperial guard across the courtyard from the waiting room to the hall, amid great commotion, and led Duke Heinrich to an upper room above the great hall. The room and adjoining chamber were furnished with tapestries and a princely bed. The Duke pledged to Herr von Rosenberg, on behalf of the Emperor and on his princely honor, not to leave the room until further imperial instructions. He was served at the Emperor’s expense from a separate kitchen: fourteen dishes in the morning and twelve in the evening, with eight attendants, and each day ten pounds of wine and sufficient beer from the imperial cellar. Visitors were allowed to see him. Four guards kept watch over him day and night. When Herr von Rosenberg had arranged all this, he took leave of the Duke and comforted him, saying he should be patient; the Emperor would soon find another way to settle matters, and Herr von Rosenberg would help bring it about. He then returned to the Emperor.

Schweinschen, the Duke’s steward, was distraught to see his lord imprisoned and his companion, the Chancellor, sent to the White Tower. Hanns Lossatte had disappeared and did not know where to go; nevertheless, in great sorrow he followed his lord. As Herr von Rosenberg came back down the stairs by the great hall, he asked his marshal, Mettig, where his countryman Schweinschen, the steward from Liegnitz, was. Schweinschen heard him and feared he too would suffer the same fate. He pushed through the crowd and presented himself to Herr von Rosenberg, who knew him and immediately offered his hand. Herr von Rosenberg said he deeply sympathized with the Duke and with Schweinschen, but that Schweinschen need not fear imperial displeasure: the Emperor was gracious. He had asked for him so he could tell him that the Emperor would kindly provide the Duke’s meals with eight attendants, and that Mettig would show him where to collect them. Schweinschen could also expect Herr von Rosenberg’s favor and assistance and, if he wished to stay with him, should entrust himself to Mettig. The steward, at first so frightened, was relieved by these words and warmly thanked Herr von Rosenberg; he was shown where to obtain food and drink for his imprisoned prince.

For several days Duke Heinrich remained troubled and sorrowful over what had happened. The constant visits and consolations of other lords somewhat eased his distress and gave him hope that the situation would not last long. Nevertheless, he sent all his household, except the eight attendants mentioned, back to Liegnitz, including the steward, whom he instructed to keep the household in good order and attend carefully to the Duchess and the young lady. When the steward had no money for expenses and wanted to travel to Liegnitz, he had to pawn his chains to pay for himself and the others. At their leave-taking the Duke was sorrowful and wept; he had been told he would be kept for a time at the house in Liegnitz and took comfort in thinking that he too would soon go there. When the steward reached Liegnitz and told the Duchess and the young lady what had happened to their husband and father, they were greatly shocked and grieved. They had to commend the matter to God and the highest authority, console themselves, and hope for improvement.
